table.brief: University rankings: University / Country / Score (Teaching, Research, Citations, Industry) / Overall rank

understanding.purpose: Compare the top seven universities by overall rank and four component scores, with country as context.
understanding.reading: Readers identify a university, follow its row across to compare scores and rank, and scan down individual score columns to compare institutions. On a phone, horizontal scrolling separates some of those comparisons from the university names.
groups: University and Country identify each institution and provide context.
Teaching, Research, Citations and Industry are parallel measures under the shared Score header and should have comparable widths.
Overall rank summarizes position and should remain easy to distinguish from the component scores.
keep_intact: University names as recognizable word sequences, without splitting individual words where possible.
Country names and individual numeric scores.
Rank numbers and the individual words in column headers.
may_wrap: University names can wrap at spaces; longer names can use multiple lines.
United Kingdom and United States can wrap between words.
Overall rank can wrap between its two words.
The two-tier score header already creates height that can accommodate wrapping in University, Country and Overall rank.

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Combine r1B’s narrower University column with r1A’s wrapping Country column. This preserves intact words and the parallel score widths while bringing more of Research into the first viewport and reducing total scrolling.

acceptable.name: r0B
acceptable.note: Give university names and countries more room for easier row identification at a total width of 693px, trading a longer scroll for less wrapping.

acceptable.name: r1A
acceptable.note: Give University 20px more than r0A to improve name wrapping while retaining compact Country and intact score headings. This tests whether a modest width increase improves row rhythm without pushing scores as far away as r0B.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Keep the compact University column and give Country enough space for its values on one line. This tests a different tradeoff: shorter rows for names that fit on one line, at the cost of moving the score group farther offscreen.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Give university names more room to test whether shorter names form clearer row labels and whether reduced wrapping justifies the additional scrolling. Keep country names wrapped and the score columns comparable.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Try a middle ground: give university names 20px more than r2A while retaining the intact country and score headers. This may improve name wrapping at a smaller cost to the initially visible Research column.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Test the alternative of keeping country names on one line while retaining the compact university column. This makes the context column easier to scan and may shorten rows where the university name also fits on one line, at the cost of showing less score data initially.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Use a compact 450px table to reduce scrolling while retaining room for numeric scores, accepting splits in long university names and score headers.
bad.why: University names, countries, and score headers break within words. The resulting tall, uneven rows make the table harder to scan despite reducing horizontal scrolling.

rationale: r2A keeps university names and country names intact while showing two score values for each row in the initial viewport. The four score columns have similar widths suited to their shared role, and their headers remain intact. Its horizontal overflow is substantial, but it is the smallest among the candidates without mid-word splits.

general: Preserve recognizable words and row identifiers so readers can scan rows and compare values reliably.
Give columns with the same analytical role a consistent rhythm, while allocating space according to their content.
Judge horizontal scrolling alongside what the initial viewport reveals and how well the complete table reads.
specific: The repeated two-word country names can wrap naturally without increasing the height of rows already driven by university names.
The score headers set a useful minimum width for their columns, even though the numeric values themselves are short.

tradeoffs: Wider university columns make several names easier to read and can shorten the table, but leave less score data visible initially and increase scrolling. A wider country column keeps country names on one line but adds little benefit to rows already made tall by university names.
uncertain: The ranges are approximate design tolerances, not browser-tested limits; simultaneous changes may alter wrapping or the initial viewport. Designers may reasonably prefer r2B's more readable university names over r2A's greater initial score visibility.

critique.good: University names and country names wrap at word boundaries, while scores and score headings stay intact. The first viewport shows the institution, country, Teaching score and most of Research, giving readers useful context before scrolling. The score columns have suitably similar widths.
critique.problems: Massachusetts and California each occupy three lines, making those rows taller. The viewport cuts through Research, and Citations, Industry and rank require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 130px University column leaves 109px for text, just enough for the longest individual word but not enough to shorten every name. The full table is 626px wide.

critique.good: The wider University column gives several names more natural line breaks and reduces California to two lines. Words, scores and headings stay intact.
critique.problems: The table gains substantial width for only a modest reduction in height. The first viewport shows just the beginning of Teaching, leaving almost all score comparisons beyond the initial view. Country still wraps onto two lines.
critique.cause: University expands to 180px and Country to 100px, pushing the score group 68px farther right than in r0A. The 79px of text space in Country is still too narrow for either country name on one line.

critique.good: The compact width brings most of the four score columns into the first viewport and reduces the distance needed to reach rank.
critique.problems: Broken words in institution names, country names and headings make the table difficult to scan. The fragmented headings weaken the parallel score group, and several rows become excessively tall. Rank still requires scrolling.
critique.cause: University has only 79px of text space, Country 49px, and each score column 34px. These widths are below the longest unbreakable words in those columns.

critique.good: University names remain recognizable, country names wrap at spaces, and the four score columns have comparable widths. Rows remain easy to follow across the visible portion.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through Research, and reaching the later scores and rank requires substantial horizontal scrolling. Several shorter university names occupy two lines, leaving unused space beside their text.
critique.cause: The 150px University column and 82px Country column use 232px before the scores begin. The score columns are already close to the widths needed to keep their headers intact.

critique.good: Country names fit on one line, and university names and score headers remain intact. The repeated single-line country entries are easy to scan.
critique.problems: The wider Country column creates empty space in rows whose height is set by the university name. Less of Research is visible initially, and the table requires more scrolling than r1A without reducing its height.
critique.cause: Country grows to 132px while University shrinks to 130px. The extra country width prevents wrapping but does not shorten the tallest university rows.

critique.good: The compact university column keeps every word intact while leaving Teaching fully visible and most of Research visible at first sight. Country names wrap naturally, and the score columns have consistent, readable proportions.
critique.problems: Several short university names occupy two lines, while the two technology institutes occupy three. The remaining score columns and rank require substantial horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 130px university column leaves 109px for text, just enough for the longest word but too narrow for many name sequences. The intact score headers require columns of roughly 81–88px each.

critique.good: The wider university column gives several names more natural line breaks and reduces the California institute to two lines. Country names and score headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The extra width does not shorten most rows because the country names still take two lines. It also leaves only Teaching fully visible, with Research beginning at the viewport edge, and increases the scrolling distance.
critique.cause: The 180px university column uses 50px more than r2A, while the 82px country column continues to set a two-line minimum for most rows.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r0C.why: Several university names, country names and score headers split inside words. Most scores fit initially, but the broken labels make rows harder to read.

r2A.why: University and country names wrap at word boundaries, and the visible score headings remain intact. Only part of the score group is initially visible, so comparison requires scrolling.

ref_auto.why: The visible columns preserve words and give university names a readable rhythm. Much of the score group and the rank require horizontal scrolling.

ref_equal.why: The whole table fits, but university names, country names, headers and some decimal scores break across lines. The resulting tall rows make identification and comparison difficult.

r0B.why: The generous university column keeps several names on one line, but only one score column is initially visible; the rest of the scores and rank require more scrolling.

r1A.why: University and country names wrap cleanly, with the first score fully visible. The next score column is cut by the viewport, and the remaining measures require scrolling.

raw.unsure: B and C appear almost identical in the visible area. The supplied images do not show the full widths or contents beyond their right edges, so I cannot reliably compare their total scrolling costs or judge the off-screen columns.

r0B.why: University names and countries wrap at word boundaries, and the generous name column makes rows easy to scan. Only the first score is visible initially, so comparison requires horizontal scrolling.

r2A.why: Names and countries remain intact, while Teaching and much of Research appear in the initial viewport. The narrower name column adds some wrapping but preserves a clear row rhythm.

r0C.why: More score columns appear at first, but university names, countries and score headers split within words, making both row identification and column comparison harder.

ref_auto.why: The visible columns balance readable names and countries with a useful view of Teaching and Research. Word-boundary wrapping keeps the rows coherent, though the remaining scores require scrolling.

r1A.why: Names and countries wrap cleanly, but the extra width given to University leaves Research cut off at the viewport edge without visibly reducing the number of lines in the longer names.

ref_equal.why: The whole table fits, but names, headers, countries and even decimal scores break across lines. The resulting tall rows make identification and comparison very difficult.

raw.unsure: B and D appear nearly identical in the visible portion. The supplied images do not show the full table beyond the right edge, so I cannot assess their remaining columns or total scrolling distance.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
